units.title: What is measured
units.summary: The share of a country's electricity generation that comes from solar, per year. Data from 2000 on comes from Ember; Our World in Data processes and publishes it under CC BY.

claims.text: Electricity data from 2000 onwards comes from Ember.

refs.quote: Electricity data from 2000 onwards (and from 1990 onwards for European countries, including Turkey) comes from Ember.

claims.text: Our World in Data publishes its data under the Creative Commons BY license.

refs.quote: All data, visualizations, and code produced by Our World in Data are completely open access under the Creative Commons BY license.

units.title: A tenfold rise in eleven years
units.summary: The world's solar share rose from 0.8% in 2014 to 8.7% in 2025, rising every single year.

claims.text: World solar share was 0.8% in 2014 and 8.7% in 2025.
The share roughly doubled every three to four years: 2.6% (2019) to 5.6% (2023), 4.6% (2022) to 8.7% (2025).

refs.note: World rows; ratios of the plotted values

units.title: Big economies range from 7% to 25%
units.summary: Among large economies in 2025, Chile, Spain and the Netherlands get over a fifth of their electricity from solar; the UK and US under a tenth.

claims.text: In 2025 Chile's solar share was 25.1%, the United Kingdom's 6.6%.

units.title: The top of the ranking is small grids
units.summary: In 2024 the highest shares were in small systems such as the Cook Islands (50%) and Namibia (35%): a few installations move a small grid a lot.

claims.text: The Cook Islands' solar share was 50% in 2024.
Small grids reach high shares with few installations, so they are not comparable to large economies.

units.title: How far to trust it
units.summary: 2025 covers about half as many countries and regions as 2024; the measure is electricity, not all energy; and generation share says nothing about installed capacity or cost.

claims.text: The dataset has 228 rows for 2024 but 114 for 2025.
Electricity is only part of total energy use, so solar's share of all energy is smaller.
